headline: Meta pitches itself as a world-connecting mission company that has quietly pivoted from social idealism to AI and hardware ambition.
identity: Meta has consistently valued speed and impact, a civilizational-scale mission to connect people, and — for a significant stretch — diversity and belonging as explicit organizational commitments. The DEI and belonging language, which peaked sharply in 2020–2021 with phrases like 'Diversity is a must-have for Facebook, not an option' and a full suite of affinity-group copy, has retreated markedly by 2023–2025; the 2026 snapshot shows inclusion scores near their lowest in the dataset, with careers copy dominated entirely by product showcases (AR glasses, Llama, Meta AI) and no DEI register detected at all. Meanwhile, the altruism and mission framing has shifted register: the 2009–2018 copy promised 'a more open world' and 'social value'; by 2023–2025 it reads more as technology stewardship ('we are stewards of our company and our mission') and AI-era inspiration.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are energized by large-scale technical ambition — 'building the future of AI openly and responsibly,' shipping things that are 'not just good, but also awe-inspiring' — and comfortable in a culture that explicitly prizes speed ('we build and learn faster than anyone else'), directness ('willing to have hard conversations'), and collective accountability over individual autonomy.

sections.heading: From 'Move Fast and Break Things' to 'Awe-Inspiring' Execution
sections.body:
The earliest careers copy (2009–2013) is the most nakedly performance-oriented in the dataset. The 2009 page opens with 'We need help from people who like to move fast, tackle the big stuff, and have an immediate impact,' and the 2013 page quotes the 'move fast and break things' mantra directly. Performance z-scores were at their highest in 2009 (1.49) and 2013 (1.50).

Through 2016–2018 the language softened toward connection and community — 'Connecting the world takes every one of us,' 'people are at the heart of every connection we build' — and performance scores dipped below the peer average. The 2022–2023 pages mark a return to high-performance framing: 'The pace is fast and the challenges are enormous, but this is how we thrive,' 'we build and learn faster than anyone else,' and 'It's a self-starter culture, we aren't told what to do to achieve results.' The 2023 performance z-score (1.18) is the second-highest in the full series. The 2025 copy moderates slightly, folding performance into collaboration ('our best work comes through collaboration and combining our collective skills').

sections.heading: The DEI Arc: Rise, Peak, and Retreat
sections.body:
Inclusion language was essentially absent from the careers pages through 2012 — all chunks in those years are coded 'absent' in the DEI register. It appeared explicitly in 2013 ('We're dedicated to creating an environment where people can be their authentic selves') and surged in 2016 with belonging-culture framing: 'We're dedicated to creating a workplace where everyone belongs,' 'Our culture embraces people's diverse perspectives.' The inclusion z-score hit its dataset peak in 2020 (1.83) when the page expanded to dozens of affinity-group sections (Native@, Women@, Pride@, Interfaith@, Latin@) and carried lines like 'Building a diverse team where everyone belongs is crucial to understanding where we're succeeding.'

By 2023 the explicit demographic and structural-process registers had disappeared; the copy shifted to softer collective language ('Working collectively and valuing each person for the differences we bring allows us all to do more'). The 2025 page retains one direct inclusion statement — 'Inclusion strengthens our workplace — and our world' — but frames it instrumentally around building better technology for diverse global users. The 2026 snapshot (which may reflect a near-future crawl) shows an inclusion z-score of -2.06, the lowest in the series, with zero DEI-register chunks and careers copy focused entirely on product demos. Candidates who weighted explicit DEI commitments heavily in earlier years will find the current signal considerably weaker.

sections.heading: The AI and Hardware Pivot in Self-Description
sections.body:
Techno-optimism scores were moderate-to-low from 2010 through 2022, reflecting a period when the careers copy leaned on human connection rather than technology as the primary identity. That changed in 2025, when the techno-optimism z-score jumped to 1.85 — the highest in the series — with copy foregrounding Meta Quest headsets, AR wearables, Ray-Ban AI glasses, and Llama. The 2026 snapshot pushes further still (z-score 2.70), with the entire 'We build awesome things' section devoted to product specifications: AR glasses prototypes, neural bands, multimodal AI reasoning.

The altruism facet shows a parallel shift: the 2015–2018 peak ('We're determined to build a better, more connected world for everyone,' z-scores around 1.3–1.7) has given way to a more restrained register by 2023–2024 (z-score -0.37), with mission language becoming stewardship-flavored ('We are stewards of our company and our mission') rather than civilizational. The 2025 page partially recovers altruism scores by tying AI and hardware back to human connection, but the framing is now technology-first rather than people-first.
